clinicalPearls: A benign, fleshy, reddish polypoid lesion at the posterior (dorsal) edge of the external urethral meatus
Overwhelmingly a condition of postmenopausal women, linked to oestrogen deficiency and atrophy of the urethral and vaginal tissues
Often asymptomatic and found incidentally, but may cause spotting or bleeding, dysuria, local discomfort, or pain on contact
Usually small and soft, and the diagnosis is clinical on inspection of the meatus
The main concern is distinguishing it from urethral carcinoma or prolapsed urethral mucosa, especially if the lesion is firm, irregular, ulcerated, or enlarging
Topical oestrogen and conservative measures suffice for most; surgical excision is reserved for large, symptomatic, or diagnostically uncertain lesions, with biopsy if malignancy is suspected
Recurrence can occur, and any atypical lesion should undergo histological examination
reference.pathophysiology: Urethral caruncles are thought to arise from oestrogen withdrawal after the menopause, which renders the distal urethral and periurethral mucosa atrophic and prone to eversion or prolapse at the meatus. The exposed tissue becomes chronically inflamed and vascular, forming a soft polypoid nodule composed of loose connective tissue, inflammatory cells, and a rich vascular network covered by transitional or squamous epithelium. The lesion is benign, but because it can bleed, ulcerate, and mimic malignancy, atypical examples warrant biopsy.
additionalInvestigations: Careful clinical examination of the meatus
Biopsy or excision histology when features are atypical
Cystourethroscopy if intraluminal pathology is suspected
MRI or examination under anaesthesia for suspicious lesions
redFlags: A firm, irregular, indurated, or ulcerated lesion
Failure to respond to topical oestrogen
reference.prognosis: Benign with an excellent prognosis; symptoms usually settle with conservative or topical oestrogen treatment, though caruncles may recur, and rare atypical lesions require exclusion of malignancy.
pitfalls: Assuming any meatal lesion is a benign caruncle and missing a urethral carcinoma
Excising without histology when the features are atypical
Overlooking a treatable underlying oestrogen deficiency amenable to topical therapy
Confusing it with circumferential urethral mucosal prolapse, which is managed differently
